summary: Specifies conventions for using FTP and HTTP to obtain certificates and certificate revocation lists from PKI repositories, satisfying some of the operational requirements of the Internet PKI.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2585 explains how to fetch and publish X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists using two protocols that are already everywhere: FTP and HTTP. It sets the file names, the file format and the URI that goes in the certificate, and it registers a media type for each kind of file. The aim is to give the PKI a way to distribute certificates where the Directory cannot reach.

questions: fetch certificates over http or ftp
how to fetch a certificate over http
subtitle: How to publish and fetch X.509 certificates and revocation lists with plain FTP and HTTP.

tldr.problem: Certificates and revocation lists have to reach the people holding them, but the Directory, which is the normal way to publish them, is not available in many parts of the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo fixes the conventions for using FTP and HTTP instead: a certificate goes in a file ending in .cer, a revocation list in a file ending in .crl, each holding exactly one item in DER encoding, and the location is written into the certificate as a URI. It also registers two MIME types for the same content.
tldr.outcome: Because FTP and HTTP are widely deployed and pass through many firewalls, the memo argues they are an attractive alternative to Directory access. The service only helps when the certificate is already identified by a URI, so it does not solve the problem of finding a certificate for someone whose address you know.

facts.label: File content
facts.value: Exactly one certificate or CRL, in DER format

today: RFC 2585 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It is one document in a multi-part Internet PKI standard; other documents specify further mechanisms for reaching a PKI repository.

sections.title: What the Memo Adds
sections.content:
RFC 2585 is part of a multi-part standard for the Internet Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) built on X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists. It fixes the conventions for using the File Transfer Protocol, RFC 959, and the Hypertext Transfer Protocol, RFC 2068, to obtain certificates and revocation lists from PKI repositories. Other documents cover additional mechanisms for reaching a repository, and the memo says so rather than trying to be complete on its own.

The conventions it defines satisfy some of the operational requirements of the Internet PKI, and in practice they amount to a small set of agreements: how the location of a file is written into a certificate, what the file is called, and what is inside it. That is enough for the two protocols to carry PKI material without any change to the protocols themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is one piece of a larger set of rules for running a public key infrastructure. It covers the part where certificates and revocation lists are fetched or published with FTP or HTTP, and leaves the other ways of reaching a repository to other documents.

sections.title: The PKI Model
sections.content:
The memo gives a simplified view of the architectural model the Internet PKI specifications assume. It has four kinds of component.

An end entity is a user of PKI certificates, or the end user system that a certificate names. A certification authority is the CA in the model: it issues certificates to end entities and publishes certificates and revocation lists. A registration authority, or RA, is an optional system to which a CA delegates certain management functions. A repository is a system, or a collection of distributed systems, that stores certificates and revocation lists and serves as the means of distributing them to end entities.

The arrows in the model show the flow. An end entity performs operational transactions with the repository, which is where it fetches certificates and revocation lists from. A registration authority publishes a certificate into the repository, and a certification authority publishes both certificates and revocation lists there. The end entity and the CA also take part in management transactions, and the CA publishes its own certificate to the repository, which is how the chain of trust is made available.
sections.plainLanguage: Four roles appear in the model. The end entity is the person or device that holds a certificate. The certification authority issues certificates and revocation lists. The registration authority is an optional helper that checks and processes requests for the authority. The repository is where the certificates and lists are kept and where people fetch them from.

sections.title: The Repository and Why FTP or HTTP
sections.content:
Some certification authorities require the use of on-line validation services, while others distribute revocation lists so that certificate users can do the validation themselves. In general, CAs make revocation lists available by publishing them in the Directory, and the Directory is also the normal distribution mechanism for certificates. The problem the memo names is that Directory Services are not available in many parts of the Internet today.

FTP and HTTP are offered as alternate methods for certificate and revocation list distribution. End entities and CAs may retrieve certificates and revocation lists from the repository using either protocol, end entities may publish their own certificate in the repository using either protocol, and RAs and CAs may publish certificates and revocation lists there using either protocol.

Both protocols are described as attractive alternatives to Directory access protocols for two reasons: FTP is widely deployed and anonymous FTP is accommodated by many firewalls, and the same is true of HTTP. The memo also points out a practice that the conventions support: an Internet user may publish the URI of the file holding their certificate on their business card, which is useful when there is no Directory entry for that user.

The memo is careful about what this service does not do. It satisfies the requirement to retrieve information related to a certificate that is already identified by a URI. It is not intended to satisfy the more general problem of finding a certificate for a user about whom some other information is known, such as an electronic mail address or a corporate affiliation.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates usually travel through the Directory, but the Directory does not reach everywhere. FTP and HTTP do, and both are usually allowed through firewalls, so the memo uses them instead. The catch is that the certificate has to be found by its URI first, so this cannot be used to look up a certificate from someone's email address.

sections.title: FTP Conventions
sections.content:
Within certificate extensions and CRL extensions, the URI form of GeneralName is used to give the location where issuer certificates and revocation lists may be obtained. A URI identifying the subject of a certificate may be carried in the subjectAltName certificate extension. An IA5String then describes the use of anonymous FTP to fetch the certificate or revocation list information.

The memo gives three example URIs: ftp://ftp.netcom.com/sp/spyrus/housley.cer, ftp://ftp.your.org/pki/id48.cer and ftp://ftp.your.org/pki/id48.no42.crl. The first is a certificate belonging to a person, the second a certificate file in a directory of PKI files, and the third a revocation list in the same directory.

For convenience, the names of files that contain certificates should end in .cer, and each such file holds exactly one certificate, encoded in DER format. The names of files that contain revocation lists should end in .crl, and each such file holds exactly one revocation list, also in DER format.
sections.plainLanguage: With FTP, the certificate points at its own location with an ftp URI, and the file that URI names ends in .cer and holds one certificate. A revocation list works the same way with a .crl file.

sections.title: HTTP Conventions
sections.content:
The HTTP conventions mirror the FTP ones. The URI form of GeneralName is again used inside certificate extensions and CRL extensions to say where issuer certificates and revocation lists may be obtained, and a URI identifying the subject of a certificate may be carried in the subjectAltName extension. An IA5String describes the use of HTTP to fetch the certificate or revocation list information.

The three example URIs are http://www.netcom.com/sp/spyrus/housley.cer, http://www.your.org/pki/id48.cer and http://www.your.org/pki/id48.no42.crl.

The file naming rules are the same as for FTP: a file containing a certificate should end in .cer and hold exactly one certificate in DER format, and a file containing a revocation list should end in .crl and hold exactly one revocation list in DER format. The memo repeats the reason for choosing HTTP, that it is widely deployed and accommodated by many firewalls, and repeats the limit of the service, that it finds a certificate already identified by a URI and not a certificate found from some other piece of information about a person.
sections.plainLanguage: With HTTP the rules are the same, with http URIs in place of ftp ones. A .cer file holds one certificate and a .crl file holds one revocation list, both in DER encoding.

sections.title: MIME Types for Certificates and Revocation Lists
sections.content:
Two MIME types are defined to support the transfer of certificates and revocation lists: application/pkix-cert and application/pkix-crl.

For application/pkix-cert the media type name is application and the subtype name is pkix-cert. There are no required parameters, and the one optional parameter is version, whose default value is 1. The encoding considerations say that there will be no encoding for 8-bit transports and most likely Base64 for SMTP or other 7-bit transports. The security consideration recorded is that it carries a cryptographic certificate. There is no interoperability consideration and no magic number, and the file extension given is .CER.

For application/pkix-crl the media type name is application and the subtype name is pkix-crl. Again there are no required parameters, and the optional parameter is version with a default value of 1. The encoding considerations and the interoperability considerations are the same. The security consideration recorded is that it carries a certificate revocation list, and the file extension given is .CRL.

Both types are registered with the same intended usage, COMMON, and both are intended for use by any MIME-compliant transport. The published specification given for each is the draft of the Internet PKI part 1 document, and the change controller named for both is Russ Housley.
sections.plainLanguage: Two media types are registered so that a mail program or another MIME-aware tool can recognise these files. One says the file holds a certificate, the other says it holds a revocation list. Each has an optional version number that defaults to 1.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because certificates and revocation lists are digitally signed, the memo says no additional integrity service is necessary. Neither has to be kept secret, and anonymous access to them is generally acceptable, so no privacy service is necessary either.

Two practical points follow. HTTP caching proxies are common on the Internet, and some of them do not check correctly for the latest version of an object. If a request for a certificate or revocation list goes through a misconfigured or otherwise broken proxy, the proxy may return an out-of-date response, which is a problem for revocation lists in particular since a stale list does not list recently revoked certificates.

Operators of FTP sites and web servers should authenticate the end entities that publish certificates, and the CAs and RAs that publish certificates and revocation lists. Authentication is not necessary in order to retrieve certificates and revocation lists, which are the operations that most happen.
sections.plainLanguage: The files carry their own signature, so they need no extra protection on the wire, and they need not be secret. Two things still matter. A caching proxy can hand back an out-of-date copy, which matters for revocation lists. And whoever publishes a file should be checked, although fetching one needs no check at all.
